The opinion's rule discussion is centrally about qualified immunity: "Qualified immunity shields an officer from suit when she makes a decision that, even if constitutionally deficient, reasonably misapprehends the law governing the circumstances she confronted."

reasons: The disposition supports entitlement to qualified immunity: the opinion reverses the Ninth Circuit on qualified immunity.
The opinion says Graham and Garner are "cast at a high level of generality" and that this case is not an obvious one where those standards alone clearly establish the answer.
The opinion describes the relevant inquiry as whether to shoot "a disturbed felon, set on avoiding capture through vehicular flight, when persons in the immediate area are at risk from that flight."
The opinion states that the three fact-specific cases did not squarely govern and suggested Brosseau's actions fell in the "hazy border between excessive and acceptable force."
The case is an excessive-force claim under the Fourth Amendment arising from an officer's shooting of a fleeing suspect in a vehicle.
The opinion frames the constitutional question under Tennessee v. Garner and Graham v. Connor, then refines how clearly established law applies in that use-of-force context.
residual_risks: The Court expressly did not decide whether the shooting violated the Fourth Amendment, so the role is strongest as a qualified-immunity refinement within use-of-force doctrine, not as a merits holding.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Keep use-of-force references tied to qualified immunity and clearly established law.
